content: Toki Pona is a complete language of
around 140 words. This pack teaches
all of it, from the first card to
the last.
With so few words, meaning is built
by combining simple ones. tomo tawa,
a moving structure, is a car.
ilo toki, a talking tool, is a
telephone.
Most languages are too big to finish.
This one isn't. Every word you meet
here is a piece of the whole — and
the whole is within reach.
HOW THE COURSE TEACHES
Content words come first. From the
very first cards, you build meaning
by combining them.
The grammar particles — li, e, pi, o,
la, and the rest — arrive as lessons,
each at the exact card where it first
appears. Play in order, and the
grammar meets you right on time.
Spelling is phonetic: say what you
see, and you've said it right.
500 cards. One whole language.
Let's begin.
Toki Pona has no word for 'to be' —
the doing or being word just
follows who or what it's about.
A bare mi or sina goes one step
further and skips li too - the little link
word every other subject needs:
mi pona.    = I am good. I'm fine.
sina pona.  = You are good.
THE CATCH: this only works for the
pronoun alone. Add any modifier and
li comes right back:
mi mute li pona. = We are good.
(mi mute = 'I' plus mute = 'we',
no longer a bare mi — li returns)
Every subject EXCEPT a lone mi or
sina needs li right before the word
that says what it does or is —
jan, ona, ni, or any longer phrase:
ni li pona ala pona?
= Is this good or not? Is this OK?
jan li pona.  = The person is good.
li also chains a second predicate
onto the SAME subject, no repeat:
jan li moku li lape.
= The person eats and sleeps.
(one jan, two li's, and no word
for 'and' needed at all)
o has two jobs, both about telling
or calling someone directly.
1. COMMAND (imperative): o stands
where li would go, right before
the verb.
o kama! = Come!
sina o pali. = You should work.
2. VOCATIVE: o follows whoever you
are calling out to — no li needed.
jan pona o! = Hey, good friend!
o is NOT the same word as a — that
other particle marks emotion and
emphasis, not commands.
pi bundles the describing words
after it into ONE group, so they
describe an earlier word together
instead of each stacking on alone.
WITHOUT pi, everything just stacks
flat onto the first word:
tomo pona lili = a small, good house
WITH pi, bundle a describing group:
jan pi toki pona
= person OF Toki Pona (a tokiponist)
(toki pona = one bracketed unit describing jan)
jan pi ma ante
= person of another land, foreigner
Modern usage: pi only regroups, not possession.
Toki Pona word order is head-first:
the main word leads, its modifiers
stack on afterward, in order:
jan pona   = good person, friend
tomo suli  = big building
Modifiers can stack on each other
too. mute after one means 'very':
jan pona mute = a very good friend
tomo suli mute = a huge building
English puts adjectives BEFORE the
noun (a good friend) — Toki Pona
always puts them AFTER (jan pona).
CONTENT QUESTIONS: put seme exactly
where the missing answer goes:
ni li seme?    = What is this?
sina lon seme? = Where are you?
YES/NO QUESTIONS: repeat the word
around ala, 'not':
sina pona ala pona?
= Are you good, or not? (the
classic way to ask how you are)
anu seme tags a guess, like English
'...or what?':
sina mute li kama anu seme?
= Are you all coming, or what?
A preverb sits BEFORE the main verb
and colors its meaning:
wile = want/need to   ken = can/may
kama = become, come to
sona = know how to
alasa = try to       awen = keep on
mi wile moku.  = I want to eat.
mi wile e ni: sina kama pona.
= I want this: for you to get well.
Stack the plain verb right after the
preverb — no separate conjugation,
just one extra word does the job.
